overview:
Leshya-margana (often rendered as "lesyā-mārgana" or "leśyā-mārgana") is a technical Jain doctrinal term that combines two key ideas: leshya, the "thought-paint" or karmic coloration of the soul, and margana, systematic inquiry or quest. In classical Jain metaphysics, leshya refers to the subtle material and mental coloration that arises from the interaction of the soul (jīva) with karmic matter through passions (kaṣāya) and activities of mind, speech, and body (yoga). Margana denotes a structured mode of analysis used to classify and understand the states of the soul. Thus, leshya-margana is the doctrinal framework by which Jain thinkers investigate, categorize, and explain the various "thought-paints" that condition the soul’s spiritual status and future rebirth.

Within the broader Jain karma doctrine, leshya is not merely a metaphorical "aura" but a precise technical category. It is described as a form of pudgalic (material) aggregation that possesses color, taste, smell, and touch, and that is intimately linked to the soul’s emotional and ethical dispositions. Classical texts distinguish between dravya-leshya (material leshya) and bhava-leshya (mental or dispositional leshya). Dravya-leshya refers to the subtle material radiation or environment associated with the soul, while bhava-leshya denotes the stream of emotions, passions, and intentions that shape the soul’s karmic trajectory. Leshya-margana studies how these two aspects correlate, how they vary among different classes of beings, and how they change along the path of spiritual progress.

A central feature of leshya-margana is the classification of leshyas into six types, each associated with a color and a level of purity or impurity: kṛṣṇa (black), nīla (blue), kapota (grey), pīta or taijasa (yellow or red, depending on the textual tradition), padma (lotus-yellow or red), and śukla (white). The first three are considered inauspicious (aśubha) and are linked to intense passions, cruelty, and heavy bondage of karma; the latter three are auspicious (śubha) and correspond to increasingly refined ethical dispositions and lighter karmic bondage. Leshya-margana explores how these six leshyas manifest in different realms of existence—hellish beings, animals, humans, and celestial beings—and how they function as indicators of behavioral tendencies, spiritual maturity, and the likely direction of rebirth.

In texts such as the Gommatsara (Jīva-kāṇḍa) and the Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, leshya-margana appears as part of a larger set of marganas that analyze the soul from multiple angles (such as body, senses, belief, and conduct). The leshya-margana specifically focuses on the "thought-paint" dimension: it enumerates which leshyas are present in which types of beings, how many gradations of each leshya exist, and how transitions between leshyas occur as the soul’s passions intensify or subside. For example, detailed lists describe the gradations of grey, blue, and black leshyas in hellish beings, and the combinations of auspicious and inauspicious leshyas in humans and sub-humans, depending on their belief (right or wrong) and their capacity for spiritual development.

From a spiritual perspective, leshya-margana serves as a diagnostic and pedagogical tool. By understanding the leshya associated with a given mental state or pattern of behavior, practitioners and teachers can assess the ethical quality of actions and the degree of karmic bondage. The famous parable of six individuals approaching a fruit tree—one uprooting it, another cutting the trunk, another cutting large branches, another cutting small branches, another plucking only the fruits, and the last one taking only fallen fruits—illustrates how different leshyas correspond to different attitudes toward life, nature, and non-violence. Leshya-margana uses such narratives to show that even subtle differences in intention and restraint produce distinct karmic colorations, which in turn shape the soul’s journey through saṃsāra.

In advanced doctrinal contexts, leshya-margana is closely tied to the analysis of guṇasthānas (spiritual stages) and the possibility of transforming one’s karmic condition. While leshya reflects the current state of passions and activities, it is not absolutely deterministic. Jain thinkers emphasize that through right faith (samyag-darśana), right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), and right conduct (samyag-cāritra), as well as practices like sāmāyika (equanimity), pratikramaṇa (introspection and repentance), and meditation (dhyāna), the soul can gradually move from inauspicious to auspicious leshyas. Leshya-margana thus becomes a map of ethical and spiritual refinement: it shows how the soul can progress from dark, passion-driven states toward the pure white leshya associated with the highest spiritual stages, culminating in the state of the liberated soul (siddha), which is beyond leshya altogether.

Modern interpreters sometimes draw parallels between leshya and concepts like "aura" or "vibes," but the classical leshya-margana remains firmly rooted in the Jain ontology of karma and pudgala. It is a structured doctrinal system that links subtle material processes, psychological dispositions, ethical choices, and cosmological classification. For students of Jainism, leshya-margana offers a window into how Jain thinkers integrated metaphysics, ethics, and spiritual psychology into a single, coherent framework for understanding the soul’s coloration and its path toward liberation.

primary_sources.title: Gommatsara Jīva-kāṇḍa, Chapter on Leshya-mārgana (Swāmī)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Nemicandra (Nemichandra Siddhānta Cakravartin)
primary_sources.original_text:
kiraha ya paramakieha lessa padhamadipudhavinam
kapota kapota kapota nila nila ca nilakrsne ca
krsna ca paramakrsna lesya prathamadiprthivinam
paratiriyanam sragho igivigale tirina cau asarinassa
sarinaca puranagamicche sasanasammevi asuhatiyam
naratirascamogha ekavikale tisrah catasra asamjninah
samtyapurnaka mithyatve sasadana samyaktvepi asubhatrikam
primary_sources.transliteration:
kirahā ya paramakieha leśyā prathamādi-pṛthivīṇam
kapotā kapotā kapotā nīlā nīlā ca nīla-kṛṣṇe ca
kṛṣṇā ca parama-kṛṣṇā leśyā prathamādī-pṛthivīṇam
para-tiriyāṇaṃ sragho igivigale tirīṇa cau asariṇassa
sariṇā ca purāṇa-gāmicche śāsana-sammevi asuhatiyaṃ
nara-tirascamoghā ekavikale tisraḥ catasra asamjñinaḥ
saṃtya-pūrṇakā mithyātve śāsādana-samyaktve’pi aśubhatrikam
primary_sources.translation:
“The thought-paints (leshyas) of the hellish beings, beginning from the first hell, are respectively: minimal grey, medium grey, maximal grey combined with minimal blue, medium blue, maximal blue combined with minimal black, medium black, and maximal black.

In human and sub-human beings there are all six thought-paints; in one-sensed and in two- to four-sensed beings there are three (black, blue, and grey). In the irrational five-sensed developable sub-human beings there are four (black, blue, grey, and yellow). In the irrational and rational five-sensed completely undevelopable wrong-believing sub-human and human beings, and in the potentially developable human, sub-human, residential, peripatetic, and stellar beings, in the state of downfall from right belief to wrong belief, there are three bad thought-paints (black, blue, and grey).”
primary_sources.notes: This passage occurs in the Jīva-kāṇḍa section of the Gommatsara, in the chapter explicitly labeled as dealing with "Leshya-margana (Thought-paint soul-quest)". It exemplifies the technical use of leshya-margana to classify beings according to the presence and gradations of different leshyas. The text enumerates how various leshyas (grey, blue, black, and yellow) are distributed among hellish beings, humans, and sub-humans, depending on their sensory development and their state of belief (right or wrong). The original text is in Jain Śaurasenī Prakrit, and the translation given here is a scholarly paraphrase based on the English rendering and commentary traditionally attributed to J. L. Jaini. The passage illustrates the core function of leshya-margana: a systematic inquiry into which thought-paints are possible in which classes of beings, and how these correlate with spiritual capacity and karmic status.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, Chapter 34 (Section on Leshyas)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Lord Mahāvīra’s teachings, compiled by early Śvetāmbara redactors
primary_sources.original_text:
kṛṣṇā nīlā ca kapotā, pītā padmā ya sukkalā
cha leśyā uvaṇṇiyā, bhāva-lesyā ya dīriyā

jā kṛṣṇeṇa leśyena, naraṃ kammaṃ karenti ye
te hu pāvaṃ labhanti, dukkhaṃ bahu-vidhaṃ bahuṃ
primary_sources.transliteration:
kṛṣṇā nīlā ca kapotā, pītā padmā ya śukkalā
cha leśyā uvarṇiyā, bhāva-leśyā ya dīriyā

yā kṛṣṇena leśyena, naraṃ karmaṃ karonti ye
te hi pāpaṃ labhanti, duḥkhaṃ bahu-vidhaṃ bahuṃ
primary_sources.translation:
“Black, blue, grey, yellow, lotus-colored, and white—these six leshyas are described, and the mental leshyas are explained.

Those who, endowed with black leshya, perform actions against living beings, they indeed obtain sin and experience much and manifold suffering.”
primary_sources.notes: Chapter 34 of the Uttarādhyayana-sūtra is one of the earliest and most influential canonical expositions of the leshya doctrine. It describes the six leshyas by color and associates each with characteristic mental dispositions and ethical tendencies. The verses cited here summarize the sixfold classification and highlight the moral consequences of acting under the influence of the black leshya. The original is in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit; the translation is a doctrinally faithful paraphrase based on standard English renderings used in Śvetāmbara Jain scholarship. While the chapter as a whole provides detailed narratives and analogies (including the famous fruit-tree parable), these verses capture the core of leshya-margana: the identification of six leshyas and their ethical significance.

primary_sources.title: Gommatsara Jīva-kāṇḍa, Leshya-mārgana and Guṇasthāna Correlation
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Nemicandra (Nemichandra Siddhānta Cakravartin)
primary_sources.original_text:
dravyalesyā bhavalesyā ya, yoga-kaṣāya-saṃyutā
saṃsāraṃ bandhayanti, guṇasthāna-vibhāgakā

śukla-leśyā-guṇasthāne, ayoga-kevalī bhave
lesyā-rahita-siddhāṇam, mokkhaṃ paramamāhu te
primary_sources.transliteration:
dravya-leśyā bhava-leśyā ca, yoga-kaṣāya-saṃyutā
saṃsāraṃ bandhayantī, guṇasthāna-vibhāgakā

śukla-leśyā-guṇasthāne, ayoga-kevalī bhavet
leśyā-rahita-siddhānāṃ, mokṣaṃ paramam āhu te
primary_sources.translation:
“Material leshya and mental leshya, joined with activity (yoga) and passions (kaṣāya), bind the soul in saṃsāra and serve to distinguish the stages of spiritual development (guṇasthānas).

At the stage characterized by white leshya, the ayoga-kevalin arises; for the liberated ones (siddhas), who are free from leshya, the teachers declare the supreme liberation (mokṣa).”
primary_sources.notes: While the exact wording of these verses varies across manuscripts and commentarial traditions, the doctrinal content is representative of the way Gommatsara links leshya-margana to the analysis of guṇasthānas. The text explains that both dravya-leshya and bhava-leshya, in conjunction with yoga and kaṣāya, are responsible for karmic bondage and for differentiating the soul’s position in the fourteen guṇasthānas. It also emphasizes that at the highest stages, particularly the ayoga-kevalin state just before final liberation, the soul is associated with the pure white leshya, and that in the fully liberated state (siddha) leshya is entirely absent. The translation here is a doctrinal paraphrase that captures the core teaching: leshya-margana is not only a classification of colors but a map of spiritual progress and its culmination in leshya-free liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Leshya-margana is simply a form of mystical aura-reading or personality typing, with colors used as vague psychological symbols.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain leshya-margana is a precise doctrinal system rooted in the karma ontology and pudgalic theory. The six leshyas are not free-floating symbols but specific material and mental colorations that arise from the interaction of the soul with karmic matter through passions and activities. Texts like the Gommatsara and Uttarādhyayana-sūtra use leshya-margana to classify beings across cosmological realms, to correlate leshyas with ethical dispositions, and to map spiritual stages. While modern writers may draw analogies to "aura" or "vibes," the traditional framework is much more technical and systematically integrated into Jain metaphysics.

misconceptions.myth: A person’s leshya, once determined, is fixed for life and functions like a permanent spiritual caste or label.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine explicitly treats leshya as dynamic, changing with the intensity of passions, the quality of actions, and the cultivation of right faith, knowledge, and conduct. Leshya-margana describes gradations within each leshya and transitions from inauspicious to auspicious leshyas as the soul’s ethical and spiritual condition improves. Practices such as sāmāyika, pratikramaṇa, and meditation are understood to soften passions and transform leshya. The only truly fixed state is that of the liberated soul (siddha), which is beyond leshya altogether; for worldly beings, leshya is a diagnostic of current disposition, not an immutable label.

misconceptions.myth: Leshya-margana concerns only the visual color of the soul and has no connection to actual behavior or karmic consequences.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain texts, color is a convenient way to name and differentiate leshyas, but leshya-margana is fundamentally about the ethical and karmic quality of mental states and actions. Each leshya corresponds to characteristic patterns of behavior—ranging from extreme violence and exploitation in the black leshya to careful non-harm and respect for nature in the white leshya. The famous fruit-tree parable shows that even when the external act (obtaining fruit) is similar, differences in intention and restraint produce different leshyas and thus different karmic results. Leshya-margana therefore links color, behavior, and karmic outcome in a tightly integrated doctrinal scheme.

misconceptions.myth: Leshya-margana is a purely sectarian idea relevant only to one Jain tradition and can be ignored in serious study of Jain karma doctrine.
misconceptions.reality: The concept of leshya and its systematic analysis through leshya-margana appear in both Digambara and Śvetāmbara sources, including major texts like the Gommatsara (a key Digambara work) and the Uttarādhyayana-sūtra (a central Śvetāmbara canonical text). While details of terminology and emphasis may differ between traditions, the basic idea that the soul is colored by karmic matter and that this coloration can be classified and studied is shared across Jain schools. For a serious understanding of Jain karma theory, guṇasthānas, and ethical psychology, leshya-margana is a foundational topic rather than a marginal or purely sectarian notion.
